title: Price the Commodity Cheap, Charge for the Unique
documentTitle: Internal Google Email Thread: Rubicon Margins and AdX Pricing Strategy
excerptForBlog:
What if we did something courageous that leverages the fact that we have strong buy and sell-side offerings. We drop the AdX/Demand Product margin to a transparent 5% for undifferentiated demand. What I mean by undifferentiated demand is demand a publisher can get through any SSP that doesn't leverage the use of proprietary data. The pipes that deliver that demand should charge a 'utility fee'. Let's call it 5%.

Now let's look at what happens to our business if we move to a 5% fee for undifferentiated demand. AdX Buyer Demand: Our take rate plunges from around 20% to 5%. 2018 forecast for AdX Buyer revenue is $1.8B growing at 2% yoy. Net revenue would go from $360M to $90M, for a total loss of $270M. However, demand/performance would likely increase significantly if we drop margins to 5%.

For differentiated DBM demand (i.e. demand where DBM uses proprietary Google data and targeting), AdX takes a non-transparent margin on top of the 5%. We don't disclose this margin and it's dynamic, but our average take rate may well surpass 20% for differentiated DBM demand.

The message to the market would be: AdX/DP is now charging 5% for basic demand — what is your SSP charging you? The second order effects of this strategy would be quite positive for Google, but those are best discussed in person.

[Jim Giles adds:] I think pure SSP is definitely commoditizing — ultimately, I think only SSPs that also have an ad server will survive. The combination of ad server / exchange plus data gives us cover for total costs that are higher than other exchanges.

sourceCase: United States v. Google LLC (Ad Tech)
lessonTitle: Price the Commodity Cheap, Charge for the Unique
situation: In November 2017, Google ad tech leaders debated whether to slash AdX's take rate from around 20% to a transparent 5% on 'undifferentiated demand' — demand any SSP could deliver. The pitch: signal to publishers that Google's pipes are cheap, while quietly keeping a 'non-transparent' margin on 'differentiated DBM demand' powered by Google's proprietary data. The $270M revenue hit is stated openly; the 'second order effects' are explicitly reserved for in-person discussion.
insight:
The hidden move is **price discrimination dressed as transparency**. The author sees the SSP layer commoditizing (Giles: 'pure SSP is definitely commoditizing'), so competing on that layer is a losing game. The play is to reframe the market: publicly benchmark rivals on the commodity part ('what is your SSP charging you?') where Google can undercut, while shifting the real margin onto the differentiated layer where nobody else competes — Google's own buyer data via DBM.

The deeper logic: when you own two sides of a market, you can afford to run one side at utility pricing to weaken standalone competitors, then recapture margin where you have a monopoly of capability. Giles makes the moat explicit — the ad server plus exchange plus data combination 'gives us cover for total costs that are higher than other exchanges.'
application: If your product bundles a commodity input with a proprietary one, separate them in your pricing. Publish a low, clean price on the commoditized piece to reset customer expectations and pressure single-product rivals. Earn your margin on the piece only you can deliver — and don't itemize it. Before you do this, be honest with yourself about which half is actually differentiated; if you're wrong, you've just cut your own revenue by 75%.
pullQuote: When your product bundles a commodity with something rare, price the commodity like a utility and hide your margin inside what only you can offer.
leadershipTraits: willing to trade near-term revenue for structural position
